orig_sentences: The feeling of the absurd is not, for all that, the notion of the absurd.
It lays the foundations for it, and that is all.
It is not limited to that notion, except in the brief moment when it passes judgment on the universe.
Subsequently it has a chance of going further.
It is alive; in other words, it must die or else reverberate.
So it is with the themes we have gathered together.
But there again what interests me is not works or minds, criticism of which would call for another form and another place, but the discovery of what their conclusions have in common.
Never, perhaps, have minds been so different.
And yet we recognize as identical the spiritual landscapes in which they get under way.
Likewise, despite such dissimilar zones of knowledge, the cry that terminates their itinerary rings out in the same way.
It is evident that the thinkers we have just recalled have a common climate.
To say that that climate is deadly scarcely amounts to playing on words.
Living under that stifling sky forces one to get away or to stay.
The important thing is to find out how people get away in the first case and why people stay in the second case.
This is how I define the problem of suicide and the possible interest in the conclusions of existential philosophy.
mod_sentences: The visceral feeling of the absurd is not yet the philosophical concept of the absurd.
It provides the initial foundation, nothing more.
Nor is the feeling confined to that concept, except in the brief flash when consciousness passes judgment on the universe.
From that initial spark, it has the potential to evolve.
It is a living impulse; it must either wither away or echo through one's entire existence.
The same is true of the philosophical themes we have assembled.
Yet my concern is not with critiquing specific authors or intellectual systems—which would demand a different forum—but with uncovering what their final conclusions share.
Perhaps thinkers have never been so radically different from one another.
And yet we recognize the identical spiritual terrain from which they all set out.
In the same way, despite exploring entirely different fields of knowledge, the final cry that concludes their intellectual journeys sounds the exact same note.
It is clear that these thinkers inhabit a single shared atmosphere.
To call that atmosphere lethal is no mere figure of speech.
Living under that suffocating sky forces a stark choice: flee or remain.
The essential task is to discover how people escape in the first case, and why people choose to stay in the second.
This is how I frame the question of suicide and our legitimate interest in the conclusions of existential philosophy.
pairs.move: Camus distinguishes the raw visceral experience of absurdity from its rigorous conceptualization. Existential thinkers from wildly divergent backgrounds all encounter the same lethal, suffocating realization; Camus's diagnostic goal is to determine who flees through escapism and who possesses the fortitude to remain.

orig_sentences: But first I want to detour from the direct path.
Up to now we have managed to circumscribe the absurd from the outside.
One can, however, wonder how much is clear in that notion and by direct analysis try to discover its meaning on the one hand and, on the other, the consequences it involves.
mod_sentences: First, however, I must make a necessary detour.
Until now, we have only mapped the absurd from the outside, circling its perimeter.
We must now examine the concept directly, determining precisely what it means on its own terms and what practical consequences it demands.
pairs.move: Methodological pivot. Having described the psychological symptoms of absurdity in the everyday world, Camus now shifts to an internal structural analysis of the concept itself to deduce its logical demands.

orig_sentences: If I accuse an innocent man of a monstrous crime, if I tell a virtuous man that he has coveted his own sister, he will reply that this is absurd.
His indignation has its comical aspect.
But it also has its fundamental reason.
The virtuous man illustrates by that reply the definitive antinomy existing between the deed I am attributing to him and his lifelong principles.
“It’s absurd” means “It’s impossible” but also “It’s contradictory.”
If I see a man armed only with a sword attack a group of machine guns, I shall consider his act to be absurd.
But it is so solely by virtue of the disproportion between his intention and the reality he will encounter, of the contradiction I notice between his true strength and the aim he has in view.
Likewise we shall deem a verdict absurd when we contrast it with the verdict the facts apparently dictated.
And, similarly, a demonstration by the absurd is achieved by comparing the consequences of such a reasoning with the logical reality one wants to set up.
In all these cases, from the simplest to the most complex, the magnitude of the absurdity will be in direct ratio to the distance between the two terms of my comparison.
There are absurd marriages, challenges, rancors, silences, wars, and even peace treaties.
For each of them the absurdity springs from a comparison.

I am thus justified in saying that the feeling of absurdity does not spring from the mere scrutiny of a fact or an impression, but that it bursts from the comparison between a bare fact and a certain reality, between an action and the world that transcends it.
The absurd is essentially a divorce.
It lies in neither of the elements compared; it is born of their confrontation.
mod_sentences: If I accuse an innocent person of a monstrous atrocity, or tell an honorable man that he has lusted after his own sister, he will protest that the accusation is absurd.
His moral indignation may seem almost comical.
Yet his outrage rests on solid philosophical ground.
By that reply, the honorable man highlights the irreconcilable contradiction between the crime attributed to him and the lifelong principles by which he lives.
In common speech, 'That is absurd' means both 'That is impossible' and 'That is self-contradictory.'
If I witness a soldier armed only with a sword charging a battery of machine guns, I judge his action to be absurd.

Yet his act is absurd only because of the vast disproportion between his intention and the physical reality awaiting him—the glaring contradiction between his actual strength and the objective he pursues.
In the same way, we call a judicial verdict absurd when we weigh it against the verdict demanded by the facts.
Similarly, a mathematical proof by contradiction (reductio ad absurdum) operates by comparing the logical consequences of a premise with the reality one intends to establish.
In every instance, from the mundane to the complex, the magnitude of absurdity corresponds directly to the gulf separating the two elements of the comparison.
There are absurd marriages, absurd vendettas, absurd silences, absurd wars, and even absurd peace treaties.
In each case, absurdity arises exclusively from a comparison.

I am therefore justified in asserting that the feeling of the absurd never arises from examining an isolated fact or emotion in a vacuum; it erupts from the collision between a raw fact and a surrounding reality, between a human action and the larger context that envelops it.
The Absurd is fundamentally a divorce.
It resides in neither element alone; it is born entirely of their collision.
pairs.move: The foundational definition of the Relational Absurd. Absurdity is never an inherent quality of an object, a person, or the universe in isolation; it is strictly a mathematical ratio—the friction generated by comparing human intent with recalcitrant reality.

orig_sentences: In this particular case and on the plane of intelligence, I can therefore say that the Absurd is not in man (if such a metaphor could have a meaning) nor in the world, but in their presence together.
For the moment it is the only bond uniting them.
If I wish to limit myself to facts, I know what man wants, I know what the world offers him, and now I can say that I also know what links them.
I have no need to dig deeper.
A single certainty is enough for the seeker.
He simply has to derive all the consequences from it.
mod_sentences: Applying this to human intellect, I can affirm that the Absurd exists neither within humanity (if such an expression has any meaning) nor within the universe, but strictly in their joint presence.
At present, it is the sole thread binding them together.
If I restrict myself strictly to observable facts, I know what humanity yearns for, I know what the world offers in return, and I now perceive the tension that connects them.
I have no need for metaphysical speculation beyond this.
A single rock-solid certainty is enough for any honest inquirer.
One must simply follow its consequences to the very end.
pairs.move: Epistemological minimalism. Camus refuses speculative metaphysics; he identifies the three observable elements—human longing, cosmic silence, and their mutual encounter—and vows to construct an entire ethics on this single certainty.

orig_sentences: The immediate consequence is also a rule of method.
The odd trinity brought to light in this way is certainly not a startling discovery.
But it resembles the data of experience in that it is both infinitely simple and infinitely complicated.
Its first distinguishing feature in this regard is that it cannot be divided.
To destroy one of its terms is to destroy the whole.
There can be no absurd outside the human mind.
Thus, like everything else, the absurd ends with death.
But there can be no absurd outside this world either.
And it is by this elementary criterion that I judge the notion of the absurd to be essential and consider that it can stand as the first of my truths.
The rule of method alluded to above appears here.
If I judge that a thing is true, I must preserve it.
If I attempt to solve a problem, at least I must not by that very solution conjure away one of the terms of the problem.
For me the sole datum is the absurd.
The first and, after all, the only condition of my inquiry is to preserve the very thing that crushes me, consequently to respect what I consider essential in it.
I have just defined it as a confrontation and an unceasing struggle.
mod_sentences: The immediate consequence yields a foundational rule of method.
The unusual trinity unveiled here—man, world, and the absurd—is by no means a shocking discovery.
Yet, like all empirical realities, it is simultaneously elementary and profoundly complex.
Its primary characteristic is that it cannot be dismantled.
To eliminate any single element is to annihilate the entire structure.
There is no absurd outside human consciousness.
Consequently, like all human things, the absurd vanishes with death.
Yet there can be no absurd outside this physical world either.
By this elementary criterion, I recognize the absurd as essential and establish it as my primary truth.
Here the methodological rule reveals itself in full force.
If I determine something to be true, I am obligated to preserve it.
If I attempt to resolve an existential dilemma, my proposed solution must never dissolve the very terms that define the problem.
For me, the sole given reality is the absurd.
The primary and absolute condition of my inquiry is to preserve the very reality that oppresses me, respecting what is essential to its nature.
And I have just defined that nature as an ongoing confrontation and an unyielding struggle.
pairs.move: The Law of the Indivisible Trinity. Any philosophical system that tries to 'solve' the problem of existence by eliminating either human consciousness (physical suicide) or cosmic silence (philosophical suicide / religious transcendence) violates intellectual honesty.

orig_sentences: And carrying this absurd logic to its conclusion, I must admit that that struggle implies a total absence of hope (which has nothing to do with despair), a continual rejection (which must not be confused with renunciation), and a conscious dissatisfaction (which must not be compared to immature unrest).
Everything that destroys, conjures away, or exorcises these requirements (and, to begin with, consent which overthrows divorce) ruins the absurd and devaluates the attitude that may then be proposed.
The absurd has meaning only in so far as it is not agreed to.
mod_sentences: Pursuing this absurd logic to its rigorous conclusion, I must recognize that this struggle demands three things: a total absence of hope (which is entirely distinct from despair), a permanent refusal to surrender (which must never be mistaken for resignation), and a lucid dissatisfaction (which has nothing in common with adolescent angst).

Anything that evades, dissolves, or rationalizes away these demands—above all, any consent that pacifies the divorce between mind and world—destroys the absurd and invalidates the philosophy that proposes it.
The Absurd retains its validity only so long as consciousness refuses to consent to it.
pairs.move: The Triad of Defiance: No hope (not despair), active refusal (not resignation), and lucid dissatisfaction (not adolescent angst). The Absurd collapses the instant consciousness yields or makes peace with reality.

orig_sentences: There exists an obvious fact that seems utterly moral: namely, that a man is always a prey to his truths.
Once he has admitted them, he cannot free himself from them.
One has to pay something.
A man who has become conscious of the absurd is forever bound to it.
A man devoid of hope and conscious of being so has ceased to belong to the future.
That is natural.
But it is just as natural that he should strive to escape the universe of which he is the creator.
All the foregoing has significance only on account of this paradox.
Certain men, starting from a critique of rationalism, have admitted the absurd climate.
Nothing is more instructive in this regard than to scrutinize the way in which they have elaborated their consequences.
mod_sentences: An undeniable moral reality governs human consciousness: a person is always held captive by the truths they discover.
Once an individual has acknowledged a fundamental truth, they can never truly unlearn it.
Every insight exacts its price.
Anyone who awakens to the reality of the absurd remains irrevocably bound to it.
A person stripped of hope—and fully aware of that lack—no longer belongs to the future.
This is entirely natural.
Yet it is equally natural that they should frantically attempt to flee the very universe their own awareness has exposed.
Our entire analysis derives its urgency from this central paradox.
Certain profound thinkers, beginning with a rigorous critique of rationalism, have stepped directly into the climate of the absurd.
Nothing could be more illuminating than to examine how they subsequently negotiated its consequences.
pairs.move: The cognitive trap: truths hold the mind hostage. Once lucidity dawns, you cannot un-know the Absurd. Yet the psychological terror of living without future hope immediately provokes a desperate counter-impulse to escape.

orig_sentences: Now, to limit myself to existential philosophies, I see that all of them without exception suggest escape.

Through an odd reasoning, starting out from the absurd over the ruins of reason, in a closed universe limited to the human, they deify what crushes them and find reason to hope in what impoverishes them.
That forced hope is religious in all of them.
It deserves attention.
mod_sentences: Turning specifically to existential philosophies, I observe that every single one of them, without exception, ultimately advocates escape.

By a bizarre dialectical maneuver—standing upon the ruins of reason in a closed, human-scale universe—they deify the very reality that crushes them and manufacture reasons for hope out of the exact condition that impoverishes them.
In every instance, this manufactured hope assumes an explicitly religious character.
It demands our closest scrutiny.
pairs.move: The universal indictment of existentialism. Camus formulates his central critique: existentialists rightly diagnose the failure of reason, but then make an illegitimate leap by deifying the irrational and turning their prison into a temple.

orig_sentences: I shall merely analyze here as examples a few themes dear to Chestov and Kierkegaard.
But Jaspers will provide us, in caricatural form, a typical example of this attitude.
As a result the rest will be clearer.
He is left powerless to realize the transcendent, incapable of plumbing the depth of experience, and conscious of that universe upset by failure.
Will he advance or at least draw the conclusions from that failure?
He contributes nothing new.
He has found nothing in experience but the confession of his own impotence and no occasion to infer any satisfactory principle.

Yet without justification, as he says to himself, he suddenly asserts all at once the transcendent, the essence of experience, and the superhuman significance of life when he writes: “Does not the failure reveal, beyond any possible explanation and interpretation, not the absence but the existence of transcendence?”
That existence which, suddenly and through a blind act of human confidence, explains everything, he defines as “the unthinkable unity of the general and the particular.”
Thus the absurd becomes god (in the broadest meaning of this word) and that inability to understand becomes the existence that illuminates everything.
Nothing logically prepares this reasoning.
I can call it a leap.
And paradoxically can be understood Jaspers’s insistence, his infinite patience devoted to making the experience of the transcendent impossible to realize.

For the more fleeting that approximation is, the more empty that definition proves to be, and the more real that transcendent is to him; for the passion he devotes to asserting it is in direct proportion to the gap between his powers of explanation and the irrationality of the world and of experience.
It thus appears that the more bitterly Jaspers destroys the reason’s preconceptions, the more radically he will explain the world.
That apostle of humiliated thought will find at the very end of humiliation the means of regenerating being to its very depth.
mod_sentences: By way of illustration, I will focus on key themes found in Leon Chestov and Søren Kierkegaard.
First, however, Karl Jaspers offers a caricatured, almost textbook demonstration of this intellectual maneuver.
Examining his thought will make what follows unmistakable.
Jaspers finds himself incapable of grasping transcendence, unable to plumb the depths of experience, and painfully aware of a reality shattered by failure (das Scheitern).
Does he press forward or deduce the rigorous consequences of that breakdown?
He offers no genuine resolution.
He discovers nothing in lived experience except a confession of intellectual helplessness, finding no valid grounds to deduce any reassuring principle.

Yet without justification—as he openly admits—he suddenly proclaims the transcendent, the hidden essence of experience, and the superhuman purpose of life, asking: 'Does not failure itself reveal, beyond all explanation and interpretation, not the absence but the positive presence of transcendence?'
That transcendent presence, conjured by a blind leap of faith to explain everything, he terms 'the unthinkable unity of the universal and the particular.'
In this way, the absurd is transmuted into God (in the broadest metaphysical sense), and the intellect's utter failure to comprehend is transformed into the very light that illuminates reality.
Nothing in logic justifies this conclusion.
It can only be described as a leap.
Paradoxically, this explains Jaspers's relentless, exhaustive effort to prove that direct experience of transcendence is impossible.

The more elusive that glimpse becomes, and the more vacuous its definition, the more real that transcendence appears to him—for his passion in affirming it expands in direct proportion to the chasm between human reason and cosmic silence.
Thus, the more savagely Jaspers dismantles the pretensions of reason, the more grandly he claims to explain the universe.
This apostle of humiliated intellect discovers, at the very nadir of intellectual surrender, a miraculous device to regenerate human existence from the inside out.
pairs.move: Critique of Karl Jaspers's Scheitern (failure). Jaspers turns epistemological bankruptcy into metaphysical triumph: because human reason fails to grasp the infinite, that very failure is asserted as 'proof' of divine transcendence. Failure becomes an idol.

orig_sentences: Mystical thought has familiarized us with such devices.
They are just as legitimate as any attitude of mind.
But for the moment I am acting as if I took a certain problem seriously.

Without judging beforehand the general value of this attitude or its educative power, I mean simply to consider whether it answers the conditions I set myself, whether it is worthy of the conflict that concerns me.
Thus I return to Chestov.
A commentator relates a remark of his that deserves interest: “The only true solution,” he said, “is precisely where human judgment sees no solution.
Otherwise, what need would we have of God?
We turn toward God only to obtain the impossible.
As for the possible, men suffice.”
If there is a Chestovian philosophy, I can say that it is altogether summed up in this way.

For when, at the conclusion of his passionate analyses, Chestov discovers the fundamental absurdity of all existence, he does not say: “This is the absurd,” but rather: “This is God: we must rely on him even if he does not correspond to any of our rational categories.”

So that confusion may not be possible, the Russian philosopher even hints that this God is perhaps full of hatred and hateful, incomprehensible and contradictory; but the more hideous is his face, the more he asserts his power.
His greatness is his incoherence.
His proof is his inhumanity.
One must spring into him and by this leap free oneself from rational illusions.
Thus, for Chestov acceptance of the absurd is contemporaneous with the absurd itself.
Being aware of it amounts to accepting it, and the whole logical effort of his thought is to bring it out so that at the same time the tremendous hope it involves may burst forth.
Let me repeat that this attitude is legitimate.
But I am persisting here in considering a single problem and all its consequences.
I do not have to examine the emotion of a thought or of an act of faith.
I have a whole lifetime to do that.
I know that the rationalist finds Chestov’s attitude annoying.
But I also feel that Chestov is right rather than the rationalist, and I merely want to know if he remains faithful to the commandments of the absurd.
mod_sentences: Mystical traditions have long made us familiar with such dialectical acrobatics.
As a subjective posture, they are as psychologically defensible as any other.
But for now, I proceed on the assumption that our central problem must be addressed with unflinching seriousness.

Without passing prior judgment on the moral or spiritual worth of mysticism, my sole task is to see whether it satisfies the rules of my inquiry—whether it respects the integrity of the conflict before us.
This brings me directly to Leon Chestov.
A commentator records a striking remark of his: 'The only true solution,' Chestov observed, 'is found precisely where human reason sees no solution whatever.
For if reason could solve it, why would we need God?
We turn to God only to obtain the impossible.
For what is merely possible, humanity suffices on its own.'
If there is a coherent Chestovian philosophy, it is entirely distilled in those sentences.

For when, at the climax of his ferocious critiques, Chestov uncovers the irremediable absurdity of all existence, he does not conclude: 'This is the Absurd,' but rather: 'This is God; we must cast ourselves upon Him, even if He defies every category of rational thought.'

To prevent any misunderstanding, the Russian thinker even suggests that this God may be vengeful, terrifying, incomprehensible, and contradictory; yet the more grotesque His visage appears, the more absolute His power becomes.
His grandeur is His very incoherence.
His inhumanity is the ultimate proof of His existence.
One must plunge blindly into His embrace, using this leap of faith to shatter the illusions of human reason.
For Chestov, therefore, recognizing the absurd is synonymous with surrendering to it.
To become conscious of absurdity is already to embrace it, and the entire momentum of his thought is designed to expose the Absurd only so that an immense, miraculous hope may erupt from its ashes.
I repeat: such an attitude is humanly understandable.
But my commitment here is to pursue a single, rigorous question to its ultimate conclusion.
I am not evaluating the psychological warmth of religious faith or mystical rapture.
A person has an entire lifetime for that.
I realize that the academic rationalist finds Chestov's anti-rational stance exasperating.
Yet I agree with Chestov against the complacent rationalist—and my only concern is whether he remains faithful to the iron demands of the Absurd.
pairs.move: Unmasking Leon Chestov's theological reversal. Chestov's famous aphorism ('We turn to God only to obtain the impossible') reveals the existential trick: uncovering cosmic absurdity not to face it with clarity, but to use it as an emergency springboard into divine madness.

orig_sentences: Now, if it is admitted that the absurd is the contrary of hope, it is seen that existential thought for Chestov presupposes the absurd but proves it only to dispel it.
Such subtlety of thought is a conjuror’s emotional trick.
When Chestov elsewhere sets his absurd in opposition to current morality and reason, he calls it truth and redemption.
Hence, there is basically in that definition of the absurd an approbation that Chestov grants it.

If it is admitted that all the power of that notion lies in the way it runs counter to our elementary hopes, if it is felt that to remain, the absurd requires not to be consented to, then it can be clearly seen that it has lost its true aspect, its human and relative character in order to enter an eternity that is both incomprehensible and satisfying.
If there is an absurd, it is in man’s universe.
The moment the notion transforms itself into eternity’s springboard, it ceases to be linked to human lucidity.
The absurd is no longer that evidence that man ascertains without consenting to it.
The struggle is eluded.
Man integrates the absurd and in that communion causes to disappear its essential character, which is opposition, laceration, and divorce.
This leap is an escape.
Chestov, who is so fond of quoting Hamlet’s remark: “The time is out of joint,” writes it down with a sort of savage hope that seems to belong to him in particular.
For it is not in this sense that Hamlet says it or Shakespeare writes it.
The intoxication of the irrational and the vocation of rapture turn a lucid mind away from the absurd.
To Chestov reason is useless but there is something beyond reason.
To an absurd mind reason is useless and there is nothing beyond reason.
mod_sentences: If we agree that the Absurd is the absolute antithesis of hope, it becomes obvious that Chestov invokes the Absurd only to abolish it.
Such intellectual sleight of hand is nothing more than an emotional magic trick.
When Chestov contrasts his concept of the absurd with conventional morality and logic, he renames it 'truth' and 'redemption.'
At bottom, therefore, Chestov's definition conceals a profound act of theological approval.

But if the entire force of the Absurd derives from its direct collision with our fundamental longings, and if its survival depends upon our refusal to make peace with it, then Chestov has stripped it of its authentic reality—evacuating its human, mortal character so it can enter a comforting, incomprehensible eternity.
If the Absurd exists anywhere, it exists strictly within the human realm.
The moment it is transformed into a springboard for eternity, it severs all connection with lucid human consciousness.
The Absurd ceases to be that inescapable reality that an individual confronts without yielding.
The true struggle has been dodged.
Humanity assimilates the absurd, and through that mystical communion, erases its core essence: relentless opposition, internal rupture, and divorce.
This leap is an act of desertion.
When Chestov repeatedly invokes Hamlet's lament—'The time is out of joint'—he writes it with a fierce, ecstatic hope entirely unique to himself.
Yet that is neither what Hamlet meant nor what Shakespeare wrote.
The intoxicating appeal of the irrational and the hunger for religious rapture lure the lucid intellect away from the reality of the Absurd.
For Chestov, human reason is useless because something transcendent lies beyond it.
For the lucid mind, human reason is limited—and absolutely nothing lies beyond it.
pairs.move: The core existential contrast: 'Beyond Reason' vs. 'Nothing Beyond Reason'. Chestov uses the breakdown of logic as an escape hatch into eternity. Camus restores the rigor of the Absurd: reason is ineffective against the cosmos, but there is no supernatural beyond to rescue us.

orig_sentences: This leap can at least enlighten us a little more as to the true nature of the absurd.
We know that it is worthless except in an equilibrium, that it is, above all, in the comparison and not in the terms of that comparison.
But it so happens that Chestov puts all the emphasis on one of the terms and destroys the equilibrium.
Our appetite for understanding, our nostalgia for the absolute are explicable only in so far, precisely, as we can understand and explain many things.
It is useless to negate the reason absolutely.
It has its order in which it is efficacious.
It is properly that of human experience.
Whence we wanted to make everything clear.
If we cannot do so, if the absurd is born on that occasion, it is born precisely at the very meeting-point of that efficacious but limited reason with the ever resurgent irrational.

Now, when Chestov rises up against a Hegelian proposition such as “the motion of the solar system takes place in conformity with immutable laws and those laws are its reason,” when he devotes all his passion to upsetting Spinoza’s rationalism, he concludes, in effect, in favor of the vanity of all reason.
Whence, by a natural and illegitimate reversal, to the pre-eminence of the irrational.
But the transition is not evident.
For here may intervene the notion of limit and the notion of level.
The laws of nature may be operative up to a certain limit, beyond which they turn against themselves to give birth to the absurd.
Or else, they may justify themselves on the level of description without for that reason being true on the level of explanation.
Everything is sacrificed here to the irrational, and, the demand for clarity being conjured away, the absurd disappears with one of the terms of its comparison.
The absurd man, on the other hand, does not undertake such a leveling process.
He recognizes the struggle, does not absolutely scorn reason, and admits the irrational.
Thus he again embraces in a single glance all the data of experience and he is little inclined to leap before knowing.
He knows simply that in that alert awareness there is no further place for hope.
mod_sentences: This leap of faith clarifies the genuine anatomy of the Absurd.
We already know that the Absurd possesses no validity outside an exact equilibrium—that it resides strictly in the relation between two poles, never in either pole isolated on its own.
Yet Chestov loads all the weight onto a single term, shattering the scale.
Our hunger for meaning and our yearning for the absolute are intelligible only because human reason can, in fact, explain many practical aspects of our world.
It is pointless to reject human reason entirely.
Reason has its legitimate domain where it remains genuinely effective.
That domain is the realm of direct human experience.
Because reason succeeds locally, we demand that it explain the cosmos as a whole.
When it fails to do so—and when the Absurd is born—it emerges at the exact frontier where effective yet bounded reason collides with the encroaching irrational.

When Chestov attacks the Hegelian doctrine that 'the solar system moves in accordance with immutable laws, and those laws constitute its reason,' or when he battles Spinoza's totalizing rationalism, he concludes that all human reason is utterly futile.
From that conclusion, by an effortless but illegitimate reversal, he proclaims the supreme sovereignty of the irrational.
Yet that deduction is completely invalid.
Here we must introduce the concepts of boundaries and operational levels.
The physical laws of nature may function reliably up to a specific threshold, beyond which they break down and generate absurdity.
Alternatively, natural laws may be entirely valid at the level of empirical description without offering ultimate metaphysical explanation.
Chestov sacrifices everything to the irrational; by banishing the human demand for clarity, he dissolves the Absurd by deleting one half of the equation.
The lucid absurd thinker refuses this false leveling.
He sustains the combat: he neither scorns practical reason nor denies cosmic silence.
He takes in the full spectrum of reality with an unwavering gaze, refusing to leap into the dark before he understands where he lands.
He recognizes, simply and unblinkingly, that within this heightened state of awareness, there is no longer any room for hope.
pairs.move: Refuting the false dichotomy: Rationalism vs. Irrationalism. Reason is effective within human experience, but silent on cosmic meaning. Chestov illegitimately infers that because reason cannot explain everything, it is useless and the irrational is God. Camus insists on maintaining the balance without leaping.

orig_sentences: What is perceptible in Leo Chestov will be perhaps even more so in Kierkegaard.
To be sure, it is hard to outline clear propositions in so elusive a writer.

But, despite apparently opposed writings, beyond the pseudonyms, the tricks, and the smiles, can be felt throughout that work, as it were, the presentiment (at the same time as the apprehension) of a truth which eventually bursts forth in the last works: Kierkegaard likewise takes the leap.
His childhood having been so frightened by Christianity, he ultimately returns to its harshest aspect.
For him, too, antinomy and paradox become criteria of the religious.
Thus, the very thing that led to despair of the meaning and depth of this life now gives it its truth and its clarity.
Christianity is the scandal, and what Kierkegaard calls for quite plainly is the third sacrifice required by Ignatius Loyola, the one in which God most rejoices: “The sacrifice of the intellect.”
This effect of the “leap” is odd, but must not surprise us any longer.
He makes of the absurd the criterion of the other world, whereas it is simply a residue of the experience of this world.
“In his failure,” says Kierkegaard, “the believer finds his triumph.”
mod_sentences: What was evident in Leon Chestov becomes even more pronounced in Søren Kierkegaard.
Formulating straightforward philosophical propositions from so elusive and protean an author is notoriously difficult.

Yet beneath the competing pseudonyms, the irony, and the philosophical masks, one senses across his entire corpus the intuition—and dread—of a final conclusion that explodes into the open in his late writings: Kierkegaard, too, takes the leap.
Terrified in childhood by a grim, severe Christianity, he eventually surrenders to its most unforgiving demands.
For Kierkegaard as well, logical contradiction and existential paradox become the defining hallmarks of authentic faith.
Thus, the very meaninglessness that drove him to despair over mortal life is suddenly converted into the source of its ultimate truth and divine clarity.

Christianity is defined as scandal, and what Kierkegaard explicitly demands is the third and ultimate sacrifice instituted by Ignatius of Loyola—the offering in which God takes greatest delight: the sacrifice of the intellect (sacrificium intellectus).
This consequence of the leap is grotesque, yet by now it should come as no surprise.
Kierkegaard turns the Absurd into a golden passport to the next world, whereas in truth it is merely an earthly residue of human experience in this world.
'In his earthly failure,' Kierkegaard exclaims, 'the believer discovers his eternal triumph.'
pairs.move: Critique of Søren Kierkegaard's sacrificium intellectus. Kierkegaard turns the absurd into a divine credential. By demanding the sacrifice of human intellect (following Ignatius of Loyola), he transfigures earthly defeat into heavenly salvation.

orig_sentences: It is not for me to wonder to what stirring preaching this attitude is linked.
I merely have to wonder if the spectacle of the absurd and its own character justifies it.
On this point, I know that it is not so.
Upon considering again the content of the absurd, one understands better the method that inspired Kierkegaard.
Between the irrational of the world and the insurgent nostalgia of the absurd, he does not maintain the equilibrium.
He does not respect the relationship that constitutes, properly speaking, the feeling of absurdity.
Sure of being unable to escape the irrational, he wants at least to save himself from that desperate nostalgia that seems to him sterile and devoid of implication.
But if he may be right on this point in his judgment, he could not be in his negation.

If he substitutes for his cry of revolt a frantic adherence, at once he is led to blind himself to the absurd which hitherto enlightened him and to deify the only certainty he henceforth possesses, the irrational.
The important thing, as Abbé Galiani said to Mme d’Epinay, is not to be cured, but to live with one’s ailments.
Kierkegaard wants to be cured.
To be cured is his frenzied wish, and it runs throughout his whole journal.
The entire effort of his intelligence is to escape the antinomy of the human condition.
An all the more desperate effort since he intermittently perceives its vanity when he speaks of himself, as if neither fear of God nor piety were capable of bringing him to peace.
Thus it is that, through a strained subterfuge, he gives the irrational the appearance and God the attributes of the absurd: unjust, incoherent, and incomprehensible.
Intelligence alone in him strives to stifle the underlying demands of the human heart.
Since nothing is proved, everything can be proved.
mod_sentences: I am not concerned here with the passionate theology to which this stance gives voice.
My sole task is to determine whether the reality of the Absurd and its internal logic justify such a retreat.
On that count, the answer is an unequivocal no.
Re-examining the structure of the Absurd reveals the underlying mechanism of Kierkegaard's strategy.
He fails to maintain the equilibrium between cosmic silence and the human hunger for clarity.
He violates the relational tension that alone constitutes the reality of absurdity.
Certain that he cannot escape the irrational universe, he seeks at least to purge himself of that agonizing hunger for reason, which strikes him as barren and hopeless.
But even if his psychological assessment of that torment is understandable, his philosophical renunciation is completely illegitimate.

By replacing his cry of defiance with a desperate act of religious devotion, he immediately blinds himself to the lucidity that previously guided him, deifying the irrational as his only remaining anchor.
As the Abbé Galiani once remarked to Madame d'Épinay, the essential task is not to be cured, but to learn how to live with one's affliction.
Yet Kierkegaard is desperate to be cured.
To be healed of the human condition is his manic, all-consuming obsession, pulsing through every page of his private journals.
The entire machinery of his intellect is mobilized to escape the fundamental contradiction of existence.
His struggle is made all the more frantic because he catches periodic glimpses of its futility, privately confessing that neither religious piety nor holy dread can bring him lasting peace.

Through a tortured sleight of hand, he clothes the irrational in the garments of the absurd, projecting onto God the very attributes of earthly meaninglessness: injustice, incoherence, and incomprehensibility.
His intellect operates solely to strangle the legitimate demands of the human spirit.
For once reason is abandoned and nothing can be proven, anything whatsoever can be asserted as truth.
pairs.move: Abbé Galiani's maxim: 'The point is not to be cured, but to live with one's ailments.' Kierkegaard commits philosophical suicide because he cannot bear the tension; he frantically demands a cure, baptizing cosmic incoherence as God so that he can worship it.

orig_sentences: Indeed, Kierkegaard himself shows us the path taken.
I do not want to suggest anything here, but how can one fail to read in his works the signs of an almost intentional mutilation of the soul to balance the mutilation accepted in regard to the absurd?
It is the leitmotiv of the Journal.
“What I lacked was the animal which also belongs to human destiny.… But give me a body then.”
And further on: “Oh! especially in my early youth what should I not have given to be a man, even for six months … what I lack, basically, is a body and the physical conditions of existence.”
Elsewhere, the same man nevertheless adopts the great cry of hope that has come down through so many centuries and quickened so many hearts, except that of the absurd man.
“But for the Christian death is certainly not the end of everything and it implies infinitely more hope than life implies for us, even when that life is overflowing with health and vigor.”
Reconciliation through scandal is still reconciliation.
It allows one perhaps, as can be seen, to derive hope of its contrary, which is death.
But even if fellow-feeling inclines one toward that attitude, still it must be said that excess justifies nothing.
That transcends, as the saying goes, the human scale; therefore it must be superhuman.
But this “therefore” is superfluous.
There is no logical certainty here.
There is no experimental probability either.
All I can say is that, in fact, that transcends my scale.
If I do not draw a negation from it, at least I do not want to found anything on the incomprehensible.
I want to know whether I can live with what I know and with that alone.
I am told again that here the intelligence must sacrifice its pride and the reason bow down.
But if I recognize the limits of the reason, I do not therefore negate it, recognizing its relative powers.
I merely want to remain in this middle path where the intelligence can remain clear.
If that is its pride, I see no sufficient reason for giving it up.
Nothing more profound, for example, than Kierkegaard’s view according to which despair is not a fact but a state: the very state of sin.
For sin is what alienates from God.
The absurd, which is the metaphysical state of the conscious man, does not lead to God.
Perhaps this notion will become clearer if I risk this shocking statement: the absurd is sin without God.
mod_sentences: Kierkegaard openly reveals the path he has taken.
Without overinterpreting, how can one fail to see in his writings the deliberate mutilation of his own soul, undertaken to match the surrender he made before the Absurd?
This disembodiment forms the obsessive leitmotif of his Journals.
'What I lacked was the physical animal that belongs to human destiny... Give me a body, then!'
And later: 'What would I not have given in my youth to be an ordinary man, even for six months... what I lack, fundamentally, is a body and the physical conditions of existence.'
Yet this same disembodied thinker embraces the ancient cry of hope that has consoled countless generations—all except the lucid absurd mind.

'For the Christian,' he writes, 'death is by no means the end of all things; it promises infinitely more hope than mortal life could ever offer, even when that life overflows with vitality and vigor.'
A reconciliation achieved through theological scandal remains a reconciliation nonetheless.
It allows the believer to extract ultimate hope from its absolute opposite: death.
Yet even if human empathy makes us understand that impulse, intellectual excess justifies nothing.
Religious thinkers argue: 'This mystery exceeds the human scale; therefore, it must be divine.'
But that 'therefore' is a logical fraud.
It offers zero philosophical certainty.
Nor does it possess a shred of empirical probability.
All I can legitimately state is that the mystery exceeds my mortal grasp.
While I cannot disprove the transcendent, I flatly refuse to construct a philosophy upon the incomprehensible.
I want to discover whether I can live exclusively with what I know, and with nothing more.
I am warned once again that here intellect must abandon its pride and bow before the sacred.
Yet recognizing the boundaries of human reason does not mean denying its real, relative power within human experience.
I simply choose to walk this middle ridge where consciousness can maintain radical clarity.
If that insistence is called intellectual pride, I see no valid reason to renounce it.
Consider, for instance, Kierkegaard's brilliant insight that despair is not an isolated event, but a chronic spiritual condition: the exact state of sin.
In Christian theology, sin is whatever alienates the creature from God.
Yet the Absurd—which is the inescapable condition of the conscious human being—leads nowhere near God.
Perhaps the concept becomes unmistakable if I venture this definition: the Absurd is sin without God.
pairs.move: 'The Absurd is sin without God.' Camus reclaims Kierkegaard's concept of despair as estrangement. But where Kierkegaard bridges that estrangement through theological scandal, Camus refuses the leap: recognizing the limits of reason is not an excuse to bow to the incomprehensible.

orig_sentences: It is a matter of living in that state of the absurd.
I know on what it is founded, this mind and this world straining against each other without being able to embrace each other.
I ask for the rule of life of that state, and what I am offered neglects its basis, negates one of the terms of the painful opposition, demands of me a resignation.
I ask what is involved in the condition I recognize as mine; I know it implies obscurity and ignorance; and I am assured that this ignorance explains everything and that this darkness is my light.
But there is no reply here to my intent, and this stirring lyricism cannot hide the paradox from me.
One must therefore turn away.
mod_sentences: The real challenge is learning how to inhabit this condition of the Absurd.
I understand the foundation on which it rests: the human mind and the physical world locked in relentless tension, forever unable to reconcile.
I ask for an ethic by which to live within this tension, yet every system offered to me evades the foundation, denies one pole of the conflict, and demands my surrender.

I ask what is entailed by this mortal condition I recognize as my own; I know it involves darkness and finite ignorance; yet theologians assure me that this very ignorance explains everything and that this blackness is my salvation.
But this provides no honest answer to my inquiry, and no amount of poetic religious lyricism can obscure the underlying evasion.
One must therefore turn away.
pairs.move: The rejection of theological evasion. When the absurd mind asks for a practical rule of life to navigate its condition, religion offers surrender disguised as wisdom, claiming ignorance is knowledge and darkness is light. Camus firmly walks away.

orig_sentences: Kierkegaard may shout in warning: “If man had no eternal consciousness, if, at the bottom of everything, there were merely a wild, seething force producing everything, both large and trifling, in the storm of dark passions, if the bottomless void that nothing can fill underlay all things, what would life be but despair?”
This cry is not likely to stop the absurd man.
Seeking what is true is not seeking what is desirable.

If in order to elude the anxious question: “What would life be?” one must, like the donkey, feed on the roses of illusion, then the absurd mind, rather than resigning itself to falsehood, prefers to adopt fearlessly Kierkegaard’s reply: “despair.”
Everything considered, a determined soul will always manage.
mod_sentences: Kierkegaard may cry out in apocalyptic warning: 'If humanity possessed no eternal soul, if at the bedrock of reality there were only a wild, seething chaos spawning everything great and trivial in a tempest of blind forces, if a bottomless void that nothing could ever satisfy lay beneath all things, what would life be but despair?'
That terrified outcry will never deter the absurd man.
Pursuing what is true has nothing to do with pursuing what is emotionally comforting.

If escaping that anxious question—'What would life be?'—requires grazing like a stubborn donkey on the sweet roses of illusion, the absurd mind, refusing to bow to comforting falsehoods, fearlessly embraces Kierkegaard's dreaded answer: 'Despair.'
All things considered, a resolute spirit will always find a way to endure.
pairs.move: Truth vs. Desirability & The Donkey and the Roses. Kierkegaard warns that without God, existence is a bottomless void of despair. Camus accepts the challenge: if avoiding despair requires grazing like a donkey on the roses of illusion, the lucid mind chooses despair over lies.

orig_sentences: I am taking the liberty at this point of calling the existential attitude philosophical suicide.
But this does not imply a judgment.
It is a convenient way of indicating the movement by which a thought negates itself and tends to transcend itself in its very negation.
For the existentials negation is their God.
To be precise, that god is maintained only through the negation of human reason.
But, like suicides, gods change with men.
There are many ways of leaping, the essential being to leap.

Those redeeming negations, those ultimate contradictions which negate the obstacle that has not yet been leaped over, may spring just as well (this is the paradox at which this reasoning aims) from a certain religious inspiration as from the rational order.
They always lay claim to the eternal, and it is solely in this that they take the leap.
mod_sentences: At this juncture, I take the liberty of naming the existential strategy for what it is: intellectual surrender, or philosophical suicide.
Yet this designation carries no mere moralistic condemnation.
It is simply an accurate description of that intellectual maneuver by which thought abdicates its own function, attempting to transcend itself through self-annihilation.
For the existentialists, self-negation becomes their deity.
More precisely, that god survives exclusively upon the sacrifice of human reason.
Yet just as methods of physical suicide vary, so the gods men invent change with their creators.
There are countless techniques for executing the leap; the defining act is the leap itself.

Those redemptive negations and ultimate paradoxes that dissolve the obstacle before it has been confronted can emerge just as easily from rationalist philosophy as from religious fervor—and this constitutes the central paradox of our inquiry.
Both systems lay claim to the eternal, and it is in that very claim that the leap consists.
pairs.move: Naming 'Philosophical Suicide' (intellectual surrender). Camus formally coins the term: thought negating itself in order to transcend itself. Crucially, Camus reveals that the leap is not exclusively religious; rationalism can commit the identical suicide by deifying abstract concepts.

orig_sentences: It must be repeated that the reasoning developed in this essay leaves out altogether the most widespread spiritual attitude of our enlightened century: the one, based on the principle that all is reason, which aims to explain the world.
It is natural to give a clear view of the world after accepting the idea that it must be clear.
That is even legitimate, but does not concern the reasoning we are following out here.
In fact, our aim is to shed light upon the step taken by the mind when, starting from a philosophy of the world’s lack of meaning, it ends up by finding a meaning and depth in it.
The most touching of those steps is religious in essence; it becomes obvious in the theme of the irrational.
But the most paradoxical and most significant is certainly the one that attributes rational reasons to a world it originally imagined as devoid of any guiding principle.
It is impossible in any case to reach the consequences that concern us without having given an idea of this new attainment of the spirit of nostalgia.
mod_sentences: I must reiterate that the reasoning pursued in this essay deliberately bypasses the most prevalent intellectual stance of our enlightened era: the totalizing rationalism which assumes that everything is intelligible and aims to explain the universe completely.
It is easy enough to present a coherent vision of reality if one begins with the dogmatic assumption that reality must be coherent.
That classical approach is intellectually coherent on its own terms, but it has no bearing on our investigation.

Our objective is to track the precise mental pivot whereby thought begins with the world's absolute meaninglessness, only to conclude by discovering transcendent meaning and profound purpose within it.
The most poignant of these maneuvers is religious, exemplified by the cult of the irrational.
But the most paradoxical and revealing maneuver is the rationalist one: attributing rational necessity to a cosmos initially recognized as utterly devoid of any guiding purpose.
We cannot evaluate the final consequences of the Absurd without examining this sophisticated triumph of intellectual escapism.
pairs.move: The taxonomy of intellectual evasion. Having analyzed religious evasion (deifying the irrational via Jaspers, Chestov, and Kierkegaard), Camus now targets rationalist evasion: philosophies that begin by acknowledging chaos, but sneak cosmic order back in through the side door.

orig_sentences: I shall examine merely the theme of “the Intention” made fashionable by Husserl and the phenomenologists.
I have already alluded to it.
Originally Husserl’s method negates the classic procedure of the reason.
Let me repeat.
Thinking is not unifying or making the appearance familiar under the guise of a great principle.
Thinking is learning all over again how to see, directing one’s consciousness, making of every image a privileged place.
In other words, phenomenology declines to explain the world, it wants to be merely a description of actual experience.
It confirms absurd thought in its initial assertion that there is no truth, but merely truths.
From the evening breeze to this hand on my shoulder, everything has its truth.
Consciousness illuminates it by paying attention to it.

Consciousness does not form the object of its understanding, it merely focuses, it is the act of attention, and, to borrow a Bergsonian image, it resembles the projector that suddenly focuses on an image.
The difference is that there is no scenario, but a successive and incoherent illustration.
In that magic lantern all the pictures are privileged.
Consciousness suspends in experience the objects of its attention.
Through its miracle it isolates them.
Henceforth they are beyond all judgments.
This is the “intention” that characterizes consciousness.
But the word does not imply any idea of finality; it is taken in its sense of “direction”: its only value is topographical.
mod_sentences: I will focus specifically on the concept of 'intentionality,' made prominent by Edmund Husserl and the phenomenologists.
I have already touched upon it.
In its initial formulation, Husserl's method directly challenges the classical operations of rationalism.
Let me restate the principle: thinking does not mean synthesizing or forcing appearances under some grand metaphysical umbrella.
To think is to learn anew how to see, to direct one's attention, to transform every perceptual experience into a privileged moment of awareness.
In other words, phenomenology refuses to explain the universe; it aims solely to describe lived experience as it actually appears.
It reinforces the absurd mind in its fundamental axiom: there is no universal Truth, only localized truths.
From the cool evening breeze to this hand resting upon my shoulder, every single phenomenon possesses its own distinct reality.
Consciousness does not invent reality; it illuminates it simply by attending to it.
The mind does not construct the object of its knowledge; it focuses like a lens, acting as pure attention—resembling, in Henri Bergson's metaphor, a magic lantern spotlighting a slide.
The difference is that there is no overarching screenplay, only an unfolding sequence of disparate, disconnected images.
Inside that magic lantern, every projection holds equal dignity.
Consciousness suspends its chosen objects within lived experience.
Through this act of focus, it isolates them from the background.
Henceforth, they stand beyond all reductive metaphysical judgments.
This is the 'intentionality' that defines consciousness.
The term carries no implication of cosmic purpose or ultimate teleology.
It designates pure mental orientation: its function is entirely descriptive and topographical.
pairs.move: Phenomenology's initial promise. Husserl's concept of intentionality initially appears compatible with the Absurd: it rejects grand metaphysical unifications, replaces universal 'Truth' with localized 'truths', and restricts itself to describing lived experience (the magic lantern).

orig_sentences: At first sight, it certainly seems that in this way nothing contradicts the absurd spirit.

That apparent modesty of thought that limits itself to describing what it declines to explain, that intentional discipline whence result paradoxically a profound enrichment of experience and the rebirth of the world in its prolixity are absurd procedures.
At least at first sight.
For methods of thought, in this case as elsewhere, always assume two aspects, one psychological and the other metaphysical.
Thereby they harbor two truths.
If the theme of the intentional claims to illustrate merely a psychological attitude, by which reality is drained instead of being explained, nothing in fact separates it from the absurd spirit.
It aims to enumerate what it cannot transcend.
It affirms solely that without any unifying principle thought can still take delight in describing and understanding every aspect of experience.
The truth involved then for each of those aspects is psychological in nature.
It simply testifies to the “interest” that reality can offer.
It is a way of awaking a sleeping world and of making it vivid to the mind.
But if one attempts to extend and give a rational basis to that notion of truth, if one claims to discover in this way the “essence” of each object of knowledge, one restores its depth to experience.
For an absurd mind that is incomprehensible.

Now, it is this wavering between modesty and assurance that is noticeable in the intentional attitude, and this shimmering of phenomenological thought will illustrate the absurd reasoning better than anything else.
For Husserl speaks likewise of “extra-temporal essences” brought to light by the intention, and he sounds like Plato.
All things are not explained by one thing but by all things.
I see no difference.
To be sure, those ideas or those essences that consciousness “effectuates” at the end of every description are not yet to be considered perfect models.
But it is asserted that they are directly present in each datum of perception.
There is no longer a single idea explaining everything, but an infinite number of essences giving a meaning to an infinite number of objects.
The world comes to a stop, but also lights up.
Platonic realism becomes intuitive, but it is still realism.
Kierkegaard was swallowed up in his God; Parmenides plunged thought into the One.
But here thought hurls itself into an abstract polytheism.
But this is not all: hallucinations and fictions likewise belong to “extra-temporal essences.”
In the new world of ideas, the species of centaurs collaborates with the more modest species of metropolitan man.
mod_sentences: At first glance, nothing in this methodology seems to contradict the spirit of the Absurd.

That apparent intellectual humility—content to describe what it refuses to explain—and that disciplined focus which paradoxically restores the rich, kaleidoscopic variety of the physical world are authentic absurd strategies.
At least, so it seems on the surface.
For philosophical methods always possess two dimensions: an empirical psychological side and an underlying metaphysical side.
Consequently, they harbor two competing truths.
If intentionality merely represents an empirical attitude—exhausting the richness of reality instead of explaining it away—nothing separates it from the absurd stance.
It simply catalogues what it cannot transcend.
It demonstrates that even without a grand unifying principle, the human mind can still take joy in observing and clarifying every facet of experience.
The truth belonging to each phenomenon remains strictly psychological.
It simply bears witness to the fascinating texture that reality presents to our senses.
It awakens a somnolent world, making it burst into vivid life before the mind.
But the moment one attempts to universalize that insight—claiming to extract an eternal 'essence' from every perceived object—one smuggles metaphysical depth back into existence.
To the lucid absurd mind, that move is completely unjustifiable.

This perpetual oscillation between empirical modesty and dogmatic certainty defines phenomenology, and this intellectual double-dealing provides the clearest possible case study in philosophical suicide.
For when Husserl begins speaking of 'extra-temporal essences' uncovered by intentionality, he sounds indistinguishable from Plato.
Whether reality is explained by a single supreme Form or by an infinity of Forms makes zero practical difference.
The metaphysical trap is identical.
Admittedly, the essences that consciousness isolates through description are not presented as transcendent heavenly archetypes.
Yet Husserl claims they are eternally present within every single perceptual datum.
Instead of one monistic Idea explaining reality, we are given an infinite pantheon of eternal essences conferring meaning upon an infinite catalog of objects.
The physical world is arrested in freeze-frame, bathed in artificial metaphysical light.
Platonic realism has been made intuitive, but it remains Platonic realism.
Kierkegaard drowned consciousness in his God; Parmenides dissolved it into the cosmic One.
Husserl hurls thought into an abstract polytheism.
Worse still, hallucinations, dreams, and imaginary creatures are granted their own 'extra-temporal essences.'
In this bizarre intellectual heaven, the mythical species of centaurs enjoys equal metaphysical standing with the ordinary office worker.
pairs.move: The Polytheism of Essences: Husserl as Inverted Plato. Phenomenology begins modestly by describing appearances, but then commits a rationalist leap by declaring every appearance an 'extra-temporal essence.' Husserl creates an abstract pantheon where centaurs and office workers share eternal Platonic reality.

orig_sentences: For the absurd man, there was a truth as well as a bitterness in that purely psychological opinion that all aspects of the world are privileged.
To say that everything is privileged is tantamount to saying that everything is equivalent.
But the metaphysical aspect of that truth is so far-reaching that through an elementary reaction he feels closer perhaps to Plato.
He is taught, in fact, that every image presupposes an equally privileged essence.
In this ideal world without hierarchy, the formal army is composed solely of generals.
To be sure, transcendency had been eliminated.
But a sudden shift in thought brings back into the world a sort of fragmentary immanence which restores to the universe its depth.
mod_sentences: For the absurd mind, there was both profound truth and bitter irony in the psychological insight that all phenomena are equally privileged.
To affirm that every experience is privileged is simply another way of saying that all experiences are metaphysically equivalent.
Yet Husserl's metaphysical inflation of that insight is so extravagant that it involuntarily drives the thinker back into the arms of Plato.
We are informed that behind every fleeting image lies an equally privileged, eternal essence.
In this ideal realm stripped of all hierarchy, the army consists exclusively of four-star generals.
Classical theological transcendence had supposedly been expelled from the house.
Yet by a sudden metaphysical sleight of hand, Husserl reintroduces a fragmented immanence that injects illusory cosmic depth back into the universe.
pairs.move: The Army of Generals. If every mundane perception contains an eternal essence, all hierarchy vanishes: the army consists entirely of generals. Husserl claims to eliminate transcendence, but merely fragments it into millions of miniature Platonic idols.

orig_sentences: Am I to fear having carried too far a theme handled with greater circumspection by its creators?

I read merely these assertions of Husserl, apparently paradoxical yet rigorously logical if what precedes is accepted: “That which is true is true absolutely, in itself; truth is one, identical with itself, however different the creatures who perceive it, men, monsters, angels or gods.”
Reason triumphs and trumpets forth with that voice, I cannot deny.
What can its assertions mean in the absurd world?
The perception of an angel or a god has no meaning for me.
That geometrical spot where divine reason ratifies mine will always be incomprehensible to me.
There, too, I discern a leap, and though performed in the abstract, it nonetheless means for me forgetting just what I do not want to forget.

When farther on Husserl exclaims: “If all masses subject to attraction were to disappear, the law of attraction would not be destroyed but would simply remain without any possible application,” I know that I am faced with a metaphysic of consolation.

And if I want to discover the point where thought leaves the path of evidence, I have only to reread the parallel reasoning that Husserl voices regarding the mind: “If we could contemplate clearly the exact laws of psychic processes, they would be seen to be likewise eternal and invariable, like the basic laws of theoretical natural science.
Hence they would be valid even if there were no psychic process.”
Even if the mind were not, its laws would be!
I see then that of a psychological truth Husserl aims to make a rational rule: after having denied the integrating power of human reason, he leaps by this expedient to eternal Reason.
mod_sentences: Must I worry that I have pushed a philosophical theme further than its authors intended?

I simply read Husserl's own words—paradoxical at first glance, yet strictly logical if one accepts his initial premises: 'Whatever is true is true absolutely, in itself; truth is unified and identical with itself, regardless of whether those who perceive it are men, monsters, angels, or gods.'
Through that pronouncement, I readily acknowledge, human reason triumphs and proclaims its dominion.
Yet what significance can such sweeping claims hold within the world of the Absurd?
The hypothetical perceptions of an angel or a deity are meaningless to a mortal mind.
That metaphysical coordinate where divine intellect allegedly ratifies human reason will remain forever beyond my comprehension.
Here, too, I detect a leap—and though executed in the realm of pure abstraction, it still demands that I forget the very reality I refuse to abandon.

When Husserl goes on to declare: 'If all physical matter subject to gravitation were to vanish, the law of gravity would not be destroyed, but would simply persist without physical application,' I know I am confronting a philosophy of emotional consolation.

And if I seek the exact juncture where thought abandons empirical evidence, I need only examine Husserl's identical claim regarding human consciousness: 'If we could clearly perceive the exact laws governing psychic processes, we would recognize them as eternal and invariable, like the fundamental laws of theoretical physics.
They would therefore remain fully valid even if no conscious mind existed.'
Even if consciousness did not exist, the laws of consciousness would still endure!

In this way, Husserl converts a psychological observation into a cosmic metaphysical law: having rejected the unifying power of human reason, he uses this conceptual trick to leap directly into the lap of eternal Reason.
pairs.move: Husserl's Platonic Leap into 'Eternal Reason'. Husserl claims that even if all matter and conscious minds vanished, the abstract laws of gravity and psychology would remain eternally true. Camus unmasks this as rationalist metaphysics of consolation: an abstract leap that deifies human concepts.

orig_sentences: Husserl’s theme of the “concrete universe” cannot then surprise me.
If I am told that all essences are not formal but that some are material, that the first are the object of logic and the second of science, this is merely a question of definition.
The abstract, I am told, indicates but a part, without consistency in itself, of a concrete universal.
But the wavering already noted allows me to throw light on the confusion of these terms.
For that may mean that the concrete object of my attention, this sky, the reflection of that water on this coat, alone preserve the prestige of the real that my interest isolates in the world.
And I shall not deny it.
But that may mean also that this coat itself is universal, has its particular and sufficient essence, belongs to the world of forms.
I then realize that merely the order of the procession has been changed.
This world has ceased to have its reflection in a higher universe, but the heaven of forms is figured in the host of images of this earth.
This changes nothing for me.
Rather than encountering here a taste for the concrete, the meaning of the human condition, I find an intellectualism sufficiently unbridled to generalize the concrete itself.
mod_sentences: Husserl's doctrine of the 'concrete universe' comes as no surprise.
When we are told that some essences are abstract while others are material—the former belonging to formal logic, the latter to empirical science—we are dealing merely with academic taxonomy.
The abstract, we are assured, represents merely an incomplete fragment of a larger concrete universal.
Yet the conceptual ambiguity we noted earlier allows us to untangle the confusion beneath these terms.

On one hand, this could mean that the concrete object before me—this patch of sky, the shimmering reflection of water upon this wool coat—retains the sole genuine reality that my attention carves out from the world.
And to that claim, I have no objection.
But on the other hand, it could mean that this coat is itself an eternal universal, possessing an autonomous essence that participates in the Platonic realm of Forms.
I then realize that Husserl has merely reversed the direction of the metaphysical procession.
The physical earth no longer reflects a higher transcendent heaven; instead, the heaven of Platonic Forms has been crammed into the mundane objects of this world.
For the absurd mind, this changes absolutely nothing.
Instead of finding a genuine reverence for the concrete texture of human existence, I encounter an unchecked intellectualism that universalizes and abstracts the concrete itself.
pairs.move: Critique of the 'Concrete Universal': Inverted Platonism. Husserl claims to celebrate the concrete world, but he does so by elevating everyday physical objects (a coat, a patch of sky) into eternal Platonic essences. Concrete reality is not lived; it is intellectualized and abstracted.

orig_sentences: It is futile to be amazed by the apparent paradox that leads thought to its own negation by the opposite paths of humiliated reason and triumphal reason.
From the abstract god of Husserl to the dazzling god of Kierkegaard the distance is not so great.
Reason and the irrational lead to the same preaching.
In truth the way matters but little; the will to arrive suffices.
The abstract philosopher and the religious philosopher start out from the same disorder and support each other in the same anxiety.
But the essential is to explain.
Nostalgia is stronger here than knowledge.
It is significant that the thought of the epoch is at once one of the most deeply imbued with a philosophy of the non-significance of the world and one of the most divided in its conclusions.
It is constantly oscillating between extreme rationalization of reality which tends to break up that thought into standard reasons and its extreme irrationalization which tends to deify it.
But this divorce is only apparent.
It is a matter of reconciliation, and, in both cases, the leap suffices.
It is always wrongly thought that the notion of reason is a one-way notion.
To tell the truth, however rigorous it may be in its ambition, this concept is nonetheless just as unstable as others.
Reason bears a quite human aspect, but it also is able to turn toward the divine.

Since Plotinus, who was the first to reconcile it with the eternal climate, it has learned to turn away from the most cherished of its principles, which is contradiction, in order to integrate into it the strangest, the quite magic one of participation.
It is an instrument of thought and not thought itself.
Above all, a man’s thought is his nostalgia.
mod_sentences: There is no reason to be astonished by the apparent paradox that drives thought to its own destruction through two opposite avenues: humiliated reason and triumphant reason.
From Husserl's abstract deity to Kierkegaard's blinding God, the distance is remarkably short.
Dogmatic rationalism and religious irrationalism arrive at the exact same sermon.
In truth, the path chosen hardly matters; the desperate urge to arrive at a comforting conclusion is all that counts.
The abstract metaphysician and the religious existentialist set out from the identical existential rupture, sustained by the same underlying panic.
For both, the absolute imperative is to find an ultimate explanation.
In both camps, existential nostalgia proves far stronger than lucid intellect.
It is deeply revealing that modern philosophy is simultaneously saturated with the meaninglessness of the cosmos and bitterly divided in its ultimate conclusions.
It swings continuously between the radical rationalization of reality (which atomizes the world into eternal concepts) and its radical irrationalization (which turns cosmic silence into a god).
Yet that philosophical divide is purely cosmetic.
Both sides seek reconciliation at any cost—and in both cases, the leap of faith accomplishes the trick.
We mistakenly assume that reason functions as a rigid, one-way mechanism.
In truth, no matter how rigorous its pretensions, human reason is just as malleable and volatile as any other mental faculty.
Reason possesses an earthy, human dimension, yet it can just as easily be bent toward the divine.

Ever since Plotinus first married reason to the eternal, intellect has learned to abandon its most essential anchor—the law of non-contradiction—in order to embrace the mystical, quasi-magical doctrine of participation in the One.
Reason is merely an instrument of consciousness, not consciousness itself.
And above all else, human thought is driven by its homesickness for unity.
pairs.move: The Convergence of Extremes: Plotinus, Husserl, and Kierkegaard. Triumphant reason (Husserl's eternal essences) and humiliated reason (Kierkegaard's divine irrationality) are twin escape routes born of the identical existential panic. Both sacrifice intellectual honesty to satisfy humanity's ancient nostalgia for unity.

orig_sentences: Just as reason was able to soothe the melancholy of Plotinus, it provides modern anguish the means of calming itself in the familiar setting of the eternal.
The absurd mind has less luck.
For it the world is neither so rational nor so irrational.
It is unreasonable and only that.
With Husserl the reason eventually has no limits at all.
The absurd, on the contrary, establishes its limits since it is powerless to calm its anguish.
Kierkegaard independently asserts that a single limit is enough to negate that anguish.
But the absurd does not go so far.
For it that limit is directed solely at the reason’s ambitions.
The theme of the irrational, as it is conceived by the existentials, is reason becoming confused and escaping by negating itself.
The absurd is lucid reason noting its limits.
mod_sentences: Just as metaphysical reason consoled the melancholy of Plotinus, it offers contemporary anxiety a familiar refuge within the comfort of the eternal.
The absurd mind enjoys no such luxury.
For the lucid thinker, the world is neither completely rational nor wholly irrational.
It is simply unreasonable—and nothing more.
In Husserl's hands, reason ends up acknowledging no boundaries whatever.
The absurd, by contrast, establishes definite boundaries precisely because it cannot soothe human anguish.
Kierkegaard claims on his own terms that a single encounter with the boundary is enough to abolish that anguish through faith.
But the absurd refuses to make that leap.
For the absurd mind, the boundary applies exclusively to the overreaching ambitions of human intellect.
The concept of the irrational, as brandished by the existentialists, is merely reason panicking, losing its nerve, and escaping through self-annihilation.
The Absurd, in stark contrast, is lucid reason dispassionately mapping its own limits.
pairs.move: The Definitive Distinction: Panic vs. Radical Clarity. Existential irrationalism is reason becoming confused and killing itself in terror. The Absurd, by contrast, is lucid reason calmly establishing its own boundaries without fleeing into faith or despair.

orig_sentences: Only at the end of this difficult path does the absurd man recognize his true motives.
Upon comparing his inner exigence and what is then offered him, he suddenly feels he is going to turn away.
In the universe of Husserl the world becomes clear and that longing for familiarity that man’s heart harbors becomes useless.
In Kierkegaard’s apocalypse that desire for clarity must be given up if it wants to be satisfied.
Sin is not so much knowing (if it were, everybody would be innocent) as wanting to know.
Indeed, it is the only sin of which the absurd man can feel that it constitutes both his guilt and his innocence.
He is offered a solution in which all the past contradictions have become merely polemical games.
But this is not the way he experienced them.
Their truth must be preserved, which consists in not being satisfied.
He does not want preaching.
mod_sentences: Only at the conclusion of this demanding path does the absurd man recognize his genuine motives.
Comparing his unyielding demand for clarity with what these philosophies offer him, he instinctively prepares to turn away.
